title: Abu Bakr leads the prayer
hook: too weak to lead, he asks Abu Bakr to lead the prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, the illness: nursed in Aisha's room, after a lifetime of sitting beside other people's sickbeds. Your line was visit the sick. Who did you reach? Day two hundred eighty-eight.

A parent hands over the car keys for the last time. A coach sits on the bench while someone else runs practice. Handing over the thing you always did is its own kind of hard. For years in Medina, day after day, the Prophet ﷺ had usually stood at the front of the mosque and led the prayer. Now the call went up, and he tried to get up to go, and he fainted. He came to, asked if the people had prayed, tried again, and fainted again. The people were waiting in the mosque, next door. Today, the moment he handed over.
screen: `HANDING OVER THE KEYS.` → `YEARS AT THE FRONT.` → `HE TRIES TO RISE, AND FAINTS.`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari records what he said: tell Abu Bakr to lead the people in prayer. And Aisha, Abu Bakr's own daughter, pushed back. She said her father was a tender-hearted man, that whenever he recited the Qur'an he wept, and if he stood in the Prophet's place the people wouldn't be able to hear him for his crying. The Prophet repeated it. Tell Abu Bakr to lead. So for those last days, Abu Bakr stood at the front, and the Prophet lay in the room next door. The word for the one who leads the prayer is imam, from a root meaning to be in front. And then there's a moment the reports treasure. One day he felt a little better and came out, leaning on two men. Abu Bakr heard him and began to step back to make room. The Prophet signaled: stay where you are. And he sat down beside Abu Bakr and prayed. Aisha's report adds that Abu Bakr then followed the Prophet's prayer, standing, and the people followed Abu Bakr's, so the man at the front was carrying the movements of the man sitting beside him. Jurists have long discussed what that means for who was leading. What the report shows is that he did not send his friend back into the rows. Muslims later read this scene in different ways. Sunni scholars have often read it as a sign pointing toward Abu Bakr leading the community after him. Shia Muslims read the succession differently and hold that the Prophet named 'Ali. Through those last days, the story shows a man who let another lead.
screen: `TELL ABU BAKR TO LEAD.` · `HE WILL WEEP, SAID AISHA.` · `IMAM — THE ONE IN FRONT.` · `STAY WHERE YOU ARE.` · then, large: `LET ANOTHER LEAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let someone else lead today. Sit, and breathe. Think of one place where you're usually in charge. The family group chat. The way the dishwasher gets loaded. The meeting, the playlist in the car, the plan for dinner. Picture handing it over to someone else for one day, and not correcting them. Notice what rises in you when you imagine it: relief, or itchiness. If you pray, you can ask for the grace to step back. The bell holds the time.
Imam. The one who leads the prayer, from a root meaning to be in front — the role the Prophet, too weak to stand, handed to his friend Abu Bakr. Today's word.
Your line: let another lead. Today, hand over one thing you always run, and sit beside it without taking it back. Day two hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: In congregational prayer Muslims follow one imam, who stands in front and whose movements everyone follows; the story of Abu Bakr leading in the Prophet's last days is often told when explaining who should lead the prayer.

myth: Aisha pushed for her father to lead the prayer
she pushed back, saying he would weep too much to be heard.
when the Prophet ﷺ came out, he sent Abu Bakr back into the rows
he signaled stay where you are and sat beside him; Abu Bakr followed his prayer, and the people followed Abu Bakr.
Sunni and Shia Muslims read the scene's meaning for succession differently
many Sunnis see a sign for Abu Bakr; Shia Muslims hold that the Prophet named 'Ali.

fork.setup: you're Abu Bakr, leading the prayer, and you hear the Prophet ﷺ come in, leaning on two men. what do you do?
options: keep going as if nothing happened.
stop the prayer to help him.
step back to give him the front.
fork.reveal: Abu Bakr began to step back, and the Prophet signaled him to stay, then sat down beside him and prayed.

original.note: Arabic: the one who leads the prayer, from a root meaning to be in front.

trapdoor: what you thought: someone filled in while the Prophet was sick.
what it means: a leader letting his friend stay at the front, and sitting beside him.
what a scholar hears: the reports in al-Bukhari, including Aisha's objection and the Prophet sitting beside Abu Bakr, are central to later Sunni and Shia discussion of succession.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 664; 687; 713 (tell Abu Bakr to lead the people; Aisha's objection; he comes out and sits beside Abu Bakr)

notes: Hadith numbers (Bukhari 664, 687, 713; Muslim 418) cited from memory; confirm. The fainting and trying again is from Bukhari 687 as remembered.
The Sunni/Shia difference on succession is stated in one sentence each, without ranking; please confirm both are described fairly.
Hook softened in review from 'for ten years ... five times a day' to 'day after day ... had usually stood at the front', since others led the prayer at times (e.g. when he traveled).

Shia scholarship also questions the Sunni reports themselves (e.g. who gave the instruction and whether the Prophet ﷺ then took over as imam); the script only says Shia read the succession differently. A Keeper may want a fuller, fair line.

Hook no longer opens 'Think of'; 'ten years' cut; stock 'think about what it takes' cut; 'many Sunni Muslims' became 'Sunni scholars have often read'; myth item matched to the report.
